The opening scenes in which the men trade anecdotes, as though two of Samuel Beckett’s tramps had been transported into a bucolic Coen brothers’comedy, exude a certain whimsical charm. But the play rapidly descends into hollow absurdism. Finally, in desperation, Rylance throws character and credibility to the wind.

cn.t: Rylance's quirky, absurdist meditation on ice-fishing divides critics between those charmed by its offbeat whimsy and poetic oddity, and those who find it self-indulgent and shapeless—though most agree it's admirably strange.
